title: Punchkin
place: Palaces and jungles of the Deccan
note: This reading copy condenses the public-domain text of “IV. Punchkin,” chiefly shortening the stepmother’s repeated attempts to starve the princesses and the prince’s long journey, while preserving its sequence, names, dialogue, and ending. Jacobs traces the tale to Mary Frere’s Old Deccan Days, told by her ayah Anna de Souza of a Lingayat family long settled at Goa. Spelling, punctuation, and page divisions are editorial. No Indian-language title is documented in the cited edition, so its English collection title is retained rather than back-translated.

rights.basis: Source edition published in 1892 and identified as public domain by Project Gutenberg.

artLabel: Balna and her son face the magician Punchkin in a palace garden.

pageArt.alt: The prince holds Punchkin’s green parrot while the magician’s prisoners return to life, in the plate from the cited 1892 edition.
Balna and her son rejoice with the seven restored princes and the people freed from enchantment.

scenes: Once upon a time there was a Raja who had seven beautiful daughters. They were all good girls; but the youngest, named Balna, was more clever than the rest. Their mother died while they were little, and the princesses took turns cooking their father’s dinner.
A Prudhan’s widow came daily to beg fire. While no one watched she threw mud into the dishes, then spoke so cunningly when the Raja discovered her that he married her and made her Ranee.

The new Ranee hated the seven princesses. She gave them scarcely any food, hoping her own daughter would take their place. The sisters wept beside their dead mother’s tomb, where a beautiful pomelo tree sprang up and fed them.

The Ranee’s daughter discovered the tree and told her mother. Pretending illness, the Ranee persuaded the Raja to destroy it. Then a little tank beside the tomb filled each morning with nourishing cream-cake; when this too was discovered, the Ranee had the tomb pulled down and the tank filled.
At last she demanded the princesses’ blood as medicine. The sorrowing Raja could not kill his daughters. He left them asleep in the jungle and brought the Ranee a deer’s blood instead.

Seven sons of a neighbouring Raja found the abandoned sisters. Each prince married one princess, and the youngest and handsomest married Balna. In time Balna had a son, beloved by all his uncles and aunts.
One day Balna’s husband went hunting and did not return. His six brothers went to seek him, but they too vanished.

Soon a man in a long black dress came begging at the palace. The servants thought him a holy Fakir, but he was the wicked magician Punchkin. He asked Balna to marry him; when she refused to leave her little son, Punchkin turned her into a black dog and led her away.
The six elder princesses found the baby alone and raised him tenderly. When he grew up, they told him how his mother and the seven princes had disappeared. He vowed to seek them.

After many adventures the young prince reached a magician’s palace. In its garden every rock and tree had once been a living person whom Punchkin had enchanted. Balna lived imprisoned in a high tower.
The prince made his way to her, and mother and son knew one another. He said, “Do not let Punchkin know who I am. Speak kindly to him, and discover whether death can touch him.”
Balna followed her son’s advice. Delighted, Punchkin believed she would at last marry him.
Balna asked, “Are you quite immortal? Can death never touch you?”

Punchkin answered, “Far away lies a desolate country covered with thick jungle. In its midst grows a circle of palm trees. Within stand six chattees full of water, piled one above another. Beneath the sixth is a cage containing a little green parrot. On the life of that parrot depends my life.”
He boasted that thousands of genii guarded the place, so no one could ever harm the bird. Balna repeated every word to her son.
The prince travelled many weary miles into the jungle. Resting beneath a tree, he saw a serpent climbing toward an eagle’s nest and killed it with his sword, saving two young eagles.
Their grateful parents said, “For many years that serpent devoured our young. Whenever you are in need, we will help you. Take these eaglets and let them be your servants.”

The young eagles bore the prince over the jungle to the circle of palms. The countless genii slept in the midday heat. The prince swooped down, overturned the six chattees, seized the green parrot, and flew away before the guardians could catch him.
The prince returned to Punchkin’s palace and sat at the door playing with the parrot. Punchkin hurried to him. “My boy, where did you get that parrot? Give it to me, I pray you.”
“I cannot give away my parrot,” answered the prince.
Frightened, the magician offered any price. The prince said, “Let the seven Raja’s sons whom you turned into rocks and trees be instantly liberated.”
Punchkin waved his wand, and Balna’s husband and his six brothers resumed their natural shapes. Still the prince held fast to the bird.
“Not so fast, my master,” said the prince. “First restore to life all whom you have imprisoned.”

Punchkin waved his wand again. The whole garden became suddenly alive: where rocks, stones, and trees had stood were Rajas, nobles, mighty men on prancing horses, jewelled pages, and troops of armed attendants.
The plate shown here, captioned “Punchkin’s Prisoners are set free,” comes from Jacobs’s 1892 edition.
“Give me my parrot!” cried Punchkin.

The prince tore off one wing of the parrot, and the magician’s right arm fell. He tore off the other, and Punchkin’s left arm fell. When he pulled away the bird’s legs, the magician fell upon his knees.
Nothing remained of him save the body and head, but still he cried, “Give me my parrot!”
“Take your parrot, then,” cried the boy. He wrung the bird’s neck and threw it at the magician; and with a fearful groan Punchkin died.
They freed Balna from the tower. She, her son, and the seven princes returned to their own country and lived very happily ever afterwards.
As for the rest of the world, every one went to his own house.
